model_name: How Washington legislative contests can renew or change representation

scope.proposal: Explain continuity and the different routes to changed representation in the 2026 legislative contests described by the supplied article: electoral renewal for a continuing officeholder, a change of party, replacement within a party, and succession after an officeholder leaves or seeks another seat.
scope.specific_reader_job: Given a district profile, identify which seat is being contested, what continuity or change is possible, how that contest connects to other seats or officeholders, and why an earlier election victory may still be followed by another election for the same incumbent.
scope.benefit: A reader can distinguish several simultaneous contests in one district and understand that partisan competition, an incumbent challenge, and an open seat are separate dimensions that can overlap.

consequential_alternative.scope: Build a candidate comparison guide for deciding whom to support.
consequential_alternative.benefit: Such a guide would connect candidate backgrounds and policy positions directly to a reader's preferences.
consequential_alternative.tradeoff: The article supplies uneven biographies and policy information. Using those details as a balanced voter guide would risk treating missing coverage as a missing position. The chosen scope instead explains contest structure without ranking candidates.

inquiry_vs_material_coverage.inquiry: The mechanisms by which the described elections could renew or change legislative representation, including connections between contests and the reported circumstances of an incumbent tenure.
inquiry_vs_material_coverage.supplied_coverage: One early article dated May 8, 2026, described as the first of two installments. It discusses selected contests in districts 3, 5, 11, 26, 29, 32, and 42, with different levels of detail.
inquiry_vs_material_coverage.boundary: The article is not a statewide inventory, a uniform platform survey, or evidence of subsequent election outcomes. Being included does not establish that a race is more competitive than an omitted race.

scope.reconsideration_after_exploration: Use the election for a particular seat as the basic unit, group contests by district, and connect contests through officeholder movements. A single district-level race record would collapse distinct House and Senate contests, particularly in districts 26, 29, and 32. On review, also distinguish an incumbent tenure from the appointment or election events supporting that tenure: a partial-term victory can be followed by another contest for the same officeholder.

source.title_as_supplied: Legislative races to watch as Washington’s election season revs up
source.use: All populated factual claims below come exclusively from the supplied article. Source locations refer to its introductory text or named district sections.

evidence_rules.supported_fact: An assertion reported in the supplied material, with its reporting date and location retained. This status does not imply independent verification.
evidence_rules.interpretation: An explanation or comparison derived from stated facts, kept outside the factual records.
evidence_rules.proposed_extension: A potentially useful structure whose factual population requires more information.
evidence_rules.unknown: Information absent, incomplete, or internally inconsistent in the supplied material. Null means unknown, not none.
evidence_rules.inheritance: A facts block's status and source location apply to every populated factual value in that block. Example identifiers and descriptive seat keys are local model identifiers, not official seat numbers.

things.purpose: Groups distinct legislative seats and supplies reported geographic or political context. District context is not itself an election forecast.

things.identity: District, chamber, and official position number when known.
things.purpose: Distinguishes the office from its current holder. When the House position number is missing, use a provisional key referring to the named holder.
Holds the dated candidate field, incumbent status, open-seat circumstances, and any special-term context. Primary and general elections are stages of the same contest.
Separates a person, their current office, and the seat they seek. Party preference and any reported ideological characterization belong to the candidacy's dated evidence.
Records retirement, appointment, a run for another office, or an election outcome. Distinguishes an announced departure or candidacy from completed succession.

Connect a person occupying a seat to the reported appointment and election events supporting that occupancy. Preserve the stated kind of term, such as partial term, separately from the fact of winning. Do not invent start dates, end dates, or the length of the next term.

relationships: A district contains several seats; a seat has a contest in an election cycle.
A person holds a seat and may separately seek that seat or another seat.
A reported departure or run for another office can explain why another contest is open.
Candidates compete within one field; same-party and different-party competition can coexist.
A claim about a person, contest, district, or event retains its source location and reporting date.
An incumbent tenure can have both an appointment and a later election in its reported history; incumbent is not a synonym for previously elected to a full term.
A past contest and a current contest can concern the same continuing officeholder. A reported partial-term election can explain why another contest follows.

comparison_dimensions.guardrail: These are overlapping dimensions, not exclusive race categories. A Democrat challenging a Democrat is not automatically a progressive challenger, and an unspecified party is not automatically an unaffiliated candidacy. Record appointment and election evidence separately when both are reported; neither a past victory nor incumbent status supplies an unstated term end.

facts.primary_advancement: The top two candidates advance to the general election.

source_conflict.handling: Preserve both reported values. The supplied material does not resolve the discrepancy, so do not calculate a definitive statewide seat-change scenario from either value.

examples.example_selection: The separate Morgan House contest described in the article is outside this small example; omission does not mean the district has only these two contests.

consequential_comparison.claim: A change of officeholder and a change of party control are distinct outcomes. Hall's contest could retain the incumbent, replace him with another Democrat, or produce a different party outcome. The Mena House contest requires a new holder because the seat is opening, but a new holder would not by itself imply a party change. Tracking seat, person, and party separately makes that distinction visible.
consequential_comparison.primary_implication: Because the reported rule advances two candidates, candidate party labels should not be treated as a promise that one nominee from each party will reach the general election.

what_the_examples_leave_untested: Two officeholders competing for one seat, as with Cindy Ryu and Jesse Salomon in the 32nd District Senate race.
A field containing only two candidates, as described for Lauren Davis and Imraan Siddiqi in the 32nd District.
How endorsements, policy differences, fundraising, or previous results explain electoral strength; the examples do not establish those causal relationships.
Post-primary field changes, completed succession, and statewide effects on party control.

Exact term boundaries and changes across multiple completed elections. The challenge case tests the reported partial-term relationship but does not supply a full legal or chronological account of Senate terms.

extensions_requiring_more_information.structure: Verified seat registry and dated candidate-field snapshots
extensions_requiring_more_information.information_needed: Official position identifiers, complete filings, withdrawals, and subsequent updates.
extensions_requiring_more_information.benefit: Connect the same seat across time without relying on a former holder's name.

extensions_requiring_more_information.information_needed: Consistent candidate statements, issue definitions, endorsement dates, and comparable fundraising periods.
extensions_requiring_more_information.benefit: Support a fairer candidate comparison while preserving the distinction between a recorded stance, an endorsement, and evidence of electoral strength.

extensions_requiring_more_information.information_needed: Verified results, a reconciled baseline for Senate membership, and authoritative term dates or election requirements where a detailed tenure timeline is needed.
extensions_requiring_more_information.benefit: Explain which possible changes occurred and how those outcomes affected the legislature.

revision_review.consequential_weakness: The original model centered on changes of representative and stored special-term circumstances as background text. That organization underexplained a consequential form of continuity: an incumbent may have won an election recently and still need to run again. A reader could see two election references without understanding the relationship between them.
revision_review.concrete_case: The 26th District section says Deb Krishnadasan won a special election in 2025 for a partial term and is on the ballot again in 2026 because that term was partial. Her earlier appointment is a further, distinct event in the same seat history.
revision_review.change_made: The scope now includes electoral renewal for continuing officeholders. An incumbent tenure context connects reported appointment and election events to the stated kind of term, and connects that history to the current contest.
revision_review.reader_benefit: The reader can explain why another election occurs without assuming an earlier victory secured a full term, that an incumbent has left office, or that a new vacancy must have arisen.
revision_review.revision_limit: The two original examples and their factual contents are retained. Candidate-field comparisons, vacancy links, and the original evidence distinctions remain usable. One brief challenge case exercises the added structure.
example_roles: The 5th District example still demonstrates overlapping competition within one field. Its existing appointment evidence now also supplies a tenure context without implying Hall previously won that seat.

The 29th District example still demonstrates connected open contests. A retirement and a run for another office explain prospective succession, while the model avoids recording an unreported successor.
The added 26th District case demonstrates electoral renewal after a partial-term victory, a relationship the original two examples did not exercise.

facts.explicit_connection: The article says Krishnadasan is on the ballot again because the special-election victory secured a partial term.

interpretation.claim: The 2025 victory and 2026 contest are compatible parts of one incumbent history. A contest renews electoral authorization without necessarily producing a different representative. The partial-term relationship explains the repeat contest; no turnover or new vacancy is needed to explain that relationship.
